issues.explanation: 'People cycling' is hard to link coherently to the rest of the profile for a refugee trauma presentation when the other triggers are funerals/graves and car sounds, and there are no corresponding memory or appraisal items suggesting bicycles or a cycling-related trauma cue. This trigger looks clinically disconnected from the stated trauma context and the rest of the network.

'I hurt myself physically to stop thinking about the event' is difficult to reconcile with the rest of the profile. In an older married male refugee with severe PTSD symptoms, self-harm can occur, but here it is the only extreme behavioral regulation item and is unsupported by the other selected strategies, memories, or appraisals. It appears clinically out of pattern relative to the otherwise avoidance/vigilance-focused presentation.

vignette:
Ravi is a 75-year-old potter, a South Asian man who fled his home country during a period of ethnic cleansing decades ago. The memory of the journey refuses to settle into language. What he carries is not a story but a series of fragments-the wet dirt of a mass grave he was forced to help dig, the sudden crack of gunfire that sounded like a car backfiring, the sight of soldiers' boots approaching as he pressed his face into the earth. These pieces do not connect; they arrive without sequence, and when they come, they feel more real than the present moment. Because the fragments arrived so vividly and without warning, they left him scanning his environment afterward, ready to catch any resemblance-a sound, a smell, a uniform-that might trigger the next one. He cannot describe them in sentences. When his wife asks what is wrong, he shakes his head. The words will not come.

Now he lives in a small American city, working clay in a studio behind his house. For years the wheel was his refuge. But after a nephew's funeral two months ago-his first visit to a cemetery since the trauma-Ravi felt something shift. Standing before the grave, the smell of turned earth and the sight of headstones collapsed into that old pit. His legs gave way. He had to be helped to the car. Since then, he has avoided any situation that might remind him of grief or endings. When an invitation to a community art show arrives, he throws it out; the thought of being praised, of feeling hopeful, frightens him in a way he cannot explain. He tells himself that hoping is dangerous, that it invites disaster. He has come to believe he is no longer capable of the steady, joyful work that once defined him. Even the slightest upset-a dish that cracks in the kiln-makes him put down his tools and walk away, certain he cannot cope with one more thing going wrong. Because he had come to believe that hope invited disaster and that he could not handle any more loss, he now registered every small hitch in his day as a warning sign-a crack in a pot, a neighbor's raised voice, a shift in light-each one confirming the world was unsafe.

The connection between his constant vigilance and the intrusions is tight. Ravi scans his environment without meaning to. When he hears a car backfire, his body seizes before his mind can catch up; the sound becomes a gunshot, and for a long moment he is back in that field. The police cruiser that parks down the street sends him into the kitchen, pulse racing. He now avoids any potential confrontation with his wife or neighbors; if a disagreement begins, he leaves the room, because arguing feels like the first step toward violence. These avoidances, however, only deepen his conviction that he is fragile, that the world is saturated with risk. His scanning makes him more sensitive; he notices a car idling, a uniformed figure, a patch of freshly turned earth, and each such perception triggers another wave of appraisal-I cannot handle this, I must be on guard-which in turn summons a fragment of memory: the taste of mud, the sound of boots.

The memories, especially the fragmented ones, dictate his behavior. He refuses to listen to the radio because news reports might mention funerals or war. He will not drive with his wife past the cemetery. The check of his surroundings has become second nature; before he steps into the hardware store, he peers through the window for any man in dark clothing. This vigilance once helped him survive the escape, but now it makes every walk feel like a patrol. And each time he avoids a positive event-an invitation to dinner, a chance to show his pottery-he reinforces the belief that he has lost himself. The old Ravi, the one who laughed and threw pots for hours, seems gone.

What finally brought him to the clinic was a morning last week when he could not bring himself to enter his studio. The clay was waiting, but the thought of facing the wheel, of feeling any pleasure, felt like a betrayal. He sat in the backyard, watching a car drive past, and he wept. His wife found him there, and for the first time in months, he let her hold his hand. He came to the appointment because he is terrified he will never work again, and because he is equally terrified that working might bring the memories roaring back. He wants to know if there is a way to be safe without hiding for the rest of his life.

violations.explanation: No paragraph conveys that negative appraisals (e.g., belief that world is dangerous) directly cause the patient to perceive or notice triggers; rather, triggers lead to appraisals.
No paragraph conveys that the trauma memory directly causes the patient to perceive or notice triggers; instead, triggers evoke memory and maladaptive strategies cause increased sensitivity.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Negative Appraisals → Triggers: No paragraph conveys that negative appraisals (e.g., belief that world is dangerous) directly cause the patient to perceive or notice triggers; rather, triggers lead to appraisals.
  e.g. "Once she had concluded that the world was fundamentally unsafe, almost anything could confirm it — a figure in her periphery, the wrong tone of voice, footsteps behind her."
  e.g. "The belief that she couldn't trust her own judgement meant that things she would once have registered and dismissed now snagged and held her attention."
  e.g. "Her conviction that it would happen again meant she moved through ordinary days as if they were mined — every ambiguity became a potential signal."
- Memory → Triggers: No paragraph conveys that the trauma memory directly causes the patient to perceive or notice triggers; instead, triggers evoke memory and maladaptive strategies cause increased sensitivity.
  e.g. "After the memory had surfaced, even the most ordinary things — a kettle whistling, a door slamming — felt like warnings she couldn't afford to ignore."
  e.g. "The intrusive image left her scanning every room she entered, cataloguing exits, tracking faces, unable to switch off."
  e.g. "Because the memory came back so vividly, she began to see threads of it everywhere: in strangers' faces, in certain times of day, in the quality of winter light."
